opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's genuinely one of the hardest problems in the field right now. Part of it is that "good" means very different things depending on what you want the model to do. A model that's great at competitive math might be kind of annoying to brainstorm with, and a model that's a wonderful creative writing partner might not be the one you want refactoring your codebase. So any single number is collapsing a lot of dimensions into one, and you lose most of the information that actually matters to people.

The second thing is that benchmarks saturate really fast now. You put out an eval, and within six months or a year the frontier models are at ninety-something percent, and then it stops telling you anything. Sometimes that's real progress, and sometimes it's contamination or people optimizing toward the benchmark, and from the outside it's hard to tell which. Goodhart's law hits really hard here.

And then a lot of what I care about, especially from the product and model behavior side, is really qualitative. How does the model feel to talk to? Does it ask the right clarifying question? Does it know when to push back? Does it get the intent behind a messy request? Those things are hard to put into a multiple-choice format. You end up relying on human preference data, or on model-graded evals where you have a model judge another model, and both of those have their own biases. Humans like longer answers and confident tone, and model graders inherit some of that too.

There's also the shift toward agentic, long-horizon tasks. When a model is doing something over an hour, using tools, browsing, writing code, there isn't one right answer anymore. There are many valid trajectories, and the environment itself is noisy. Building reproducible evals for that is really expensive.

So I don't think we'll ever have one standard. What's more realistic is a portfolio: some capability benchmarks, some task-specific evals that look like real usage, and a lot of careful qualitative testing by people who deeply understand what the model is supposed to be doing. Honestly, some of the best signal I've gotten has come from just spending a lot of time with the model and writing down where it surprises me, good or bad, and then turning those observations into evals.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's hard because evaluation is really a proxy for asking "what do you want the model to be good at," and nobody agrees on that. When I was working on model behavior and evals, the thing that struck me is that a benchmark freezes a particular opinion about what matters at a particular moment. MMLU encodes an opinion that knowledge recall across academic subjects is what intelligence looks like. Coding benchmarks encode another opinion. And those opinions go stale fast, because the frontier moves and the thing that was hard eighteen months ago is now table stakes.

The second problem is that the models themselves are moving targets in a way that makes static measurement weird. They're trained on the internet, the benchmarks are on the internet, and even when you're careful about contamination, the distribution of what people care about keeps shifting toward tasks that are open-ended. If I ask a model to help me write a research proposal, there's no single right answer to grade against. You end up needing another model, or a human, to judge, and now you've introduced the judge's taste into the measurement. Different labs have different taste, so the numbers stop being comparable.

And honestly the third thing is incentives. Every lab wants to show their model winning, so you get a natural pressure to pick the evals that favor your training recipe. It's not even malicious most of the time. You just build what you can measure, and then you measure what you built. That's why I've become much more interested in things like user studies, preference data from real usage, and evals that are deliberately hard to game, like having the model do long multi-step work where the failure modes show up only at the end. Those are messier, but I think messy and honest beats clean and meaningless.

astra-6.text:
I think the hard part is that “better” really depends on what you’re using the model for. A researcher might care about solving a difficult math problem, while someone writing with a model might care much more about tone, creativity, or whether it understands what they’re trying to say. Those are very different things to evaluate.

And even within one task, what does success mean? Does the model need to get the answer right on the first try, or can you work with it over several turns? A benchmark gives you a particular snapshot, but it doesn’t necessarily capture that whole interaction.

So I think we need multiple kinds of evaluations. You want some shared measurements so you can compare models, but you also need evaluations that reflect the actual use case. It’s hard to compress all of that into one score without losing something meaningful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that people want very different things from these models. If you’re using a model for coding, you might care about whether the code runs. If you’re using it for writing, you might care about its tone or whether it helps you express an idea. Those are very different definitions of quality, and even two people doing the same task can have different preferences.

There’s also a gap between what you can measure easily and what actually makes a model useful. A benchmark gives you a constrained task, but in practice you’re having a conversation. You clarify things, give feedback, and see whether the model adapts. So I think it’s hard to compress all of that into one number. You have to ask: what are we evaluating, and for whom?
